text: Social media platforms earn advertising money from posts built around news reporting they did not pay for, so the value created in the newsroom is collected somewhere else.
Reporting is expensive to produce, and if nobody pays for it once it reaches social media, less of it will be produced and people who get their news through social media will have less worth reading.

A large social media platform can walk away from any single news publisher, but no publisher can afford to lose the platform's traffic, so private bargaining alone will never set a fair price for news.
Social media platforms send news publishers readers for free, and publishers post their own links on those platforms voluntarily because they want the traffic.
Laws that force social media platforms to pay news publishers send most of the money to large publishers who can afford to negotiate, while small and independent outlets get little or nothing.
If social media platforms must pay for every news article they carry, they will choose which outlets are worth paying for, which puts a private company in charge of what news people see.
Ordinary people are generally better served when social media platforms show news posts without labeling, fact-checking, or removing them than when platforms do those things.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether platform labels and removals protect ordinary people from being misled or mostly replace their own judgment with the platform's.

text: A warning label on a social media news post tells people what to conclude before they have watched the footage or read the witness accounts themselves, which puts the platform's verdict in place of their own judgment.
A platform that labels or removes posts is making the same editorial choices a newsroom makes, but with far less training and no duty to answer to its readers.
When a social media platform removes a false news claim, the people who believe it tend to read the removal as proof of a cover-up, so they end up more convinced rather than less.

A social media feed with no labels or moderation still ranks posts by the reactions they get, so it pushes the most outrageous version of a story ahead of the most accurate one, and labeling is one of the few checks on that.
When a social media platform takes no responsibility for correcting false news posts, a correction, if anyone issues one at all, reaches only a small share of the people who saw the original error.

A video clip shared on social media without its surrounding context can be made to mean almost anything by the caption attached to it, and a platform label that restores the missing context helps people avoid being misled.
Journalists should generally have a legal right to refuse to reveal a confidential source's identity, except where a court finds the name is needed to prevent serious harm.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the public gains more from insiders who feel safe talking to reporters than it loses from courts that cannot compel the answer.

text: Most serious wrongdoing inside governments and companies comes to light because an insider talks, and insiders stay silent when they know the reporter can be made to name them.
A reporter who can be forced to identify sources is turned into an investigator for the prosecution, which is not the job the public needs the press to do.
Courts can usually get the facts they need in other ways, such as documents, other witnesses, or their own investigators, so forcing a reporter to talk is rarely the only path to the truth.
Ordinary people called as witnesses must answer a court's questions even when they promised someone secrecy, and reporters have no better claim to be excused than anyone else.

When reporters can keep sources secret unless a court finds serious harm, an official who illegally leaks classified material out of spite or for political gain usually stays hidden, so the law ends up shielding people who broke it.
Someone has to decide who counts as a journalist before a legal right to keep sources secret can apply, and that hands government a power to license the press.
A news outlet that publishes a false and damaging claim about anyone, including a public figure, should generally have to pay damages if it failed to take reasonable care to check the claim.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the greater danger is a careless press that faces no penalty or a wealthy plaintiff who can silence a careful one.

text: When a public figure ruined by a false story must prove the outlet knew the claim was false or strongly suspected it, an outlet that simply never bothered to check pays nothing.
Stepping into public life should not mean giving up the right to repair your name when a news outlet is careless with the truth, because that price keeps many capable people out of public service.
A real chance of losing in court is the one thing that reliably makes an outlet check its facts before publishing.

Wealthy and powerful people already use lawsuits to bury true stories under legal costs, and letting them win by showing only that a reporter was careless, rather than that the outlet knew the claim was false, would make those threats far more dangerous to a newsroom.
Reporters working under the threat of a lawsuit soften true statements into vague ones, so readers get less plain fact about everything, not only about the powerful.
Errors get fixed faster by public corrections and by competing outlets than by courts, which take years to decide what a reader could check in a day.
A single government-run health insurance program covering everyone would generally deliver better care at lower cost than a system of competing private insurers.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether one buyer's bargaining power and simplicity beats what competition and choice can deliver.

text: One public health insurer covering everyone spends far less on billing, marketing, and disputes over who pays than competing private insurers must, because competing is what creates those costs.
One buyer for the whole country can bargain down prices from hospitals and drug companies in a way no single private insurer can.
When there is only one insurer and every doctor accepts it, patients never lose their doctor because of a job change, a network change, or a new plan year.
With only one insurer, a patient whose treatment is denied has no other plan to switch to, so patients lose the power to take their business elsewhere.
When all health spending comes from one government budget, it competes every year with schools, roads and defense, and when money is short the gap tends to show up as longer waits for care.
The new taxes needed to pay for one public plan would hold down wages and hiring by more than the plan saves on paperwork, so the country as a whole would pay more, not less.
People should generally pay for routine medical care out of their own pockets and buy private insurance only to cover large, unexpected expenses.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether people spend more wisely on their own health when they pay directly, or simply skip the care they need.

text: Insurance exists to protect against ruin, not to pay predictable bills; running routine visits through an insurer adds paperwork and cost to every one.
People who pay for their own checkups and prescriptions shop around and ask what things cost, which pushes prices down for everyone.
Low premiums for catastrophic plans let more people afford coverage at all, instead of going without because a full plan is too expensive.
When people pay out of pocket they skip needed care along with unneeded care, and a skipped blood pressure check becomes the stroke the plan then pays for.
Patients cannot shop for medical care the way they shop for groceries; they do not know what they need, and prices are rarely posted.
Long-term illnesses like diabetes bring large bills that are steady rather than unexpected, so a plan that covers only surprises leaves the people who need the most care paying the most.
Any registered voter should be able to vote by mail without giving a reason.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether more people voting is worth losing the secrecy and custody that a polling booth provides.

text: Many working people cannot get to a polling place during open hours, and a mail ballot lets them vote without missing a shift or finding child care.
A voter filling out a mail ballot at home has time to look up candidates and ballot measures instead of guessing in a booth.

Making voters give an approved excuse to vote by mail forces them to reveal private matters like illness or travel, and officials have no practical way to check those excuses anyway, so the requirement burdens honest voters without stopping dishonest ones.
A ballot filled out at the kitchen table cannot be kept secret the way a booth keeps it, so family members, employers, or organizers can pressure the voter.
When ballots travel through the mail, election officials cannot watch them from the voter's hand to the counting room, so the chain of custody has gaps.
Mail ballots get rejected for signature mismatches and late postmarks that in-person voters never face, so some honest votes are thrown out.
Voters should generally be required to show government-issued photo identification before casting a ballot.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on how many eligible voters would be turned away against how much confidence the rule buys.

text: Nearly every other important transaction, from boarding a plane to opening a bank account, already requires photo ID, so asking for it at the polls is not a new burden.
Public trust in an election depends on people believing each voter is who they claim to be, and a photo check makes that visible to everyone in line.
A photo ID requirement removes the guesswork poll workers face when deciding whether to challenge a voter, so the process is more even from one precinct to the next.

People who are poor, elderly, or live far from a government office are the least likely to hold current photo ID, so a photo ID requirement at the polls turns away eligible citizens rather than cheats.
Voting in someone else's name is so rare that a photo ID requirement spends time and money guarding against a kind of fraud that almost never happens.
Voter registration records and signature checks already confirm who a voter is, so requiring photo ID at the polls adds a step for voters without adding real security.
The legislature, not the executive alone, should generally have to approve any sustained military action abroad.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the danger of a slow decision is greater than the danger of one person deciding alone.

text: Sending people to fight is the most serious thing a government does, so it should need the broadest agreement, not one person's judgment.
A debate in the legislature forces the case for war to be made in public, where voters can hear it and judge it.
Wars that begin without wide support tend to lose that support quickly, which leaves troops committed to a fight the country will not back.
A quick military response to an emergency often grows into a longer campaign, and stopping midway to seek the legislature's approval can leave troops in the field without clear orders.
Open debate in the legislature about a planned military action tells the enemy what the country is about to do and gives up the advantage of surprise.
Legislators avoid hard votes on war, so a rule that requires their approval often means no decision gets made at all while the situation gets worse.
A country should generally keep its military spending high in peacetime rather than cutting it once threats seem to fade.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a force kept ready deters wars or invites them, and what the money would otherwise buy.

text: Ships, aircraft, and trained crews take years to build, so a country that cuts them in calm times cannot get them back when a threat appears.
A visibly strong military discourages rivals from starting a conflict in the first place, which is far cheaper than fighting one.
Steady funding keeps the factories and skilled workers who build military equipment in business, so the country does not have to depend on others for its defense.
Every dollar spent on the military in peacetime is a dollar not spent on schools, roads, and health care that improve daily life now.
A large standing military tempts leaders to use it, drawing the country into conflicts it could have stayed out of.
Military contractors and military bases spread across every region create political pressure to keep defense spending high whether or not the actual threat justifies it.
The United Kingdom should rejoin the European single market.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether easier trade and access to workers outweigh the loss of control that comes with following rules made elsewhere.

text: British exporters selling into the European Union now face paperwork, delays, and border checks that make trade with their nearest and largest market slower and more expensive than it was when the United Kingdom was inside the single market.

Rejoining the European single market would let workers from European Union countries take jobs in the United Kingdom freely again, which would help British farms, hospitals, care homes, and hospitality businesses fill jobs they have struggled to fill.

British firms that sell in Europe already make their goods to European Union product rules, so rejoining the European single market would give the United Kingdom full access to that market while changing little about the rules its exporters actually follow.

Rejoining the European single market without rejoining the European Union would mean the United Kingdom accepting European rules and court rulings with no vote on them, which is worse than either full membership or full independence.

Rejoining the European single market would require the United Kingdom to accept free movement of people from European Union countries again, taking away its power to decide for itself who can come to live and work there.

British firms would face a second costly round of changes to their paperwork, supply chains, and product standards if the United Kingdom rejoined the European single market after they have already adjusted to trading outside it.
Japan should keep immigration low even as its population shrinks.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a shrinking, aging country can hold onto its social fabric and still keep its economy and public services running.

text: Keeping immigration low helps Japan protect the high level of trust between neighbors and strangers that its widely shared customs and language make possible.

Keeping immigration low keeps Japan's labor market tight, which pushes employers to raise wages, invest in automation, and bring more women and older people into work instead of hiring workers from abroad.

Even a large rise in immigration would only slow Japan's population decline and aging rather than stop them, so it would bring the strain of integrating many newcomers without solving the problem it is meant to solve.

Japan needs more immigrant workers because its care homes, construction sites, and farms already cannot find enough staff, and machines cannot yet bathe a patient or pick fruit well enough to close the gap.
More young immigrant workers paying taxes in Japan would help cover the cost of pensions and health care for its growing number of retirees, easing the pressure to raise taxes or cut benefits.
Rural towns across Japan are emptying out and closing schools and clinics, and immigrants willing to settle in them are the only realistic way to keep those towns alive.
Children generally do best when raised by two married parents.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether marriage itself helps children or whether it is simply the household shape that stable, better-off adults tend to choose.

text: Marriage ties both parents to a child in law from birth, with no separate paternity step, so the child's claims to support and inheritance from both parents are settled from the start.
Marriage is a public promise that makes it harder to walk away during a bad year, and children benefit from adults who stayed.
Marriage joins two extended families, so a child of married parents gains grandparents, aunts, and uncles on both sides who treat the child as fully their own.
What helps children is stability and low conflict, and a bad marriage delivers neither while trapping everyone inside it.
Children of married parents do better mostly because their households have more money and less stress, so the wedding is a sign of those advantages rather than their cause.
What children need is enough steady, caring adults, and a single parent backed by grandparents or a committed co-parent living elsewhere can supply that without any marriage.
Adults should feel free to build their family life around their own happiness rather than around tradition.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a family exists mainly for the adults who form it or for the children and elders who depend on it and get no vote.

text: Many family traditions were built on the assumption that a wife would depend on her husband's income, so they fit poorly now that both partners often work.
People stuck in roles they never chose make resentful partners and distracted parents, which serves no one, including the children.
Whether to marry, have children, or live near relatives shapes an adult's whole life, so that choice belongs to the person who has to live with it.
Families exist mostly for children and the old, who do not get a vote when the adults decide to arrange things around adult happiness.
Traditions carry hard-won lessons about what lasts and what does not, and people who discard them tend to relearn those lessons too late.
A family organized around the adults' satisfaction lasts only as long as that satisfaction does, which leaves children and aging relatives exposed when it fades.
Simple life exists on many planets in our galaxy.
bottom_line: It rests on whether plentiful planets and ingredients are enough, or whether the hard step from chemistry to a living cell and the harshness of many planets make life's start rare.

text: Planets turn out to orbit most stars, and many sit at distances where liquid water can exist, so the settings for life are abundant.
Life appeared on Earth soon after the planet cooled enough to allow it, which suggests it starts easily when conditions permit.
The chemical building blocks of life are found in comets, meteorites and clouds between the stars, so the ingredients are everywhere.
Building a self-copying cell from simple chemicals takes many steps in the right order, and no one has managed it in a lab, which suggests life's start is a rare accident rather than a routine event.
Most stars are small red dwarfs whose violent flares can strip air and water from nearby planets, so many planets that look friendly may be too harsh for even simple life to begin.

All living things on Earth share a single origin, so even on a planet as friendly as ours life seems to have started only once, which suggests that starting life is a rare event even where conditions are good.
Technology-building intelligent life has arisen on very few worlds in our galaxy besides Earth.
bottom_line: The question turns on how much weight to put on our silence in the sky against how little of it we have searched and how many chances the galaxy has had.

text: If intelligent civilizations were common, some would be far older than ours and their signals or works would likely have been noticed by now.

Complex life on Earth took most of the planet's history to appear after simple life, and technology-building intelligence appeared only once, which suggests it is an unlikely outcome rather than a natural next step.
Intelligence requires a long stretch of stable conditions, and most planets suffer collisions, radiation bursts or runaway climates before that time is up.
Searches for radio signals from other civilizations have covered only a tiny slice of the sky for a short time, so hearing nothing is weak evidence that such civilizations are rare.
Evolution on Earth produced problem-solving brains in unrelated lines, such as birds and octopuses, which suggests intelligence is a repeatable trick.
Our galaxy holds a huge number of planets and is far older than our solar system, so even if intelligence arises on only a tiny share of them, it should by now have arisen on many worlds.
Museums should generally return human remains and sacred objects to the communities descended from the people they belonged to or who made them.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether human remains and sacred objects belong first to the communities that claim them as their own dead and heritage, or to a wider public that can study and learn from them.

text: The people whose ancestors sit in a museum drawer have a stronger claim to those remains than a scholar who wants to study them, just as any family has a claim to its own dead.
Many of the human remains and sacred objects held in museums were taken during conquest or by grave robbing, so keeping them now continues a wrong rather than merely preserving history.
Communities that receive their objects back from museums often become partners in research, so returning them can expand knowledge instead of ending it.
Descent from people who lived long ago is often uncertain, and rival groups sometimes claim the same remains, so a museum that returns them risks handing a people's dead to the wrong community.
Museums keep human remains and sacred objects under controlled conditions and make them available to researchers worldwide, while a returned object may be reburied and lost to study forever.
Human remains and sacred objects shown in large public museums teach far more people about other cultures than they would if each were returned to a single community.
Archaeologists should generally excavate important sites now rather than leave them in the ground for future generations.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a site left in the ground is being saved for better tools or slowly lost to construction, looting, and weather.

text: Archaeological sites are destroyed every year by construction, farming, looting, and rising seas, so waiting to excavate often means losing the site entirely rather than saving it for later.
Knowledge dug out of an archaeological site now can shape how living people understand human history, while a site left unexcavated teaches far less to anyone alive today.
Rescue digs at threatened sites are usually rushed and narrow, so they cannot give young archaeologists the training in careful, planned research that excavating important sites provides.
Digging destroys an archaeological site as it reveals it, and every generation's methods look crude to the next, so future tools will recover far more from an untouched site.
Much excavated material is never fully studied, so digging more adds to the storage backlog faster than it adds to knowledge.
Protecting a site in place costs far less than excavating it and caring for its finds, so limited money saves more sites when spent on protection than on digging.
We should defend our fundamental freedoms, including freedom of speech.
Open dialogue is vital for informed decision-making and for holding power accountable.
The free exchange of ideas fosters creativity, scientific discovery, and cultural growth.
Free speech lets people express themselves without fear, which preserves personal dignity and self-expression.
Societies with strong protections for speech have historically thrived in liberty and innovation.
Defending free speech upholds universal principles of liberty and individual dignity.
Defending free speech encourages accountability and resistance to authoritarianism.
Defending free speech promotes a vibrant, informed society where ideas can flourish.
Defending free speech ensures long-term progress for society through dialogue and debate.
Unchecked speech can spread misinformation, incite violence, and perpetuate hate.
Free speech protections can be exploited by those in power to drown out marginalized voices.
Defending free speech may allow harmful or false narratives to go unchecked.
Defending free speech risks perpetuating systemic inequalities by empowering harmful speech.
Defending free speech could foster division or harm vulnerable populations.
Defending free speech may undermine trust in public institutions if misinformation spreads unchecked.
Supporters need individual liberties preserved.
Supporters need accountability and transparency in governance.
Supporters need open dialogue and resistance to authoritarian control, which they believe have the power to transform society.
Opponents need public safety and mental well-being protected.
Opponents need free speech kept from being exploited for harmful purposes.
Opponents need a safer, more inclusive society where speech does not endanger others.
We should defend the freedom of religion and the freedom from religion.
Defending freedom of and from religion protects personal beliefs and practices from interference by other people or the government.
Freedom of and from religion allows diverse religions and worldviews to coexist peacefully.
Defending freedom of and from religion prevents the government from imposing or endorsing religious practices.
Defending both freedom of religion and freedom from religion balances the rights of religious and non-religious people.
Defending freedom of and from religion respects individual autonomy and diverse worldviews.
Defending freedom of and from religion prevents coercion and encourages an environment of voluntary belief and expression.
Defending freedom of and from religion encourages mutual respect and coexistence in diverse societies.
Defending freedom of and from religion preserves the basic principle that government stays neutral toward religion.
Defending freedom of and from religion means balancing religious freedoms against secular interests, which can lead to disagreements and legal battles.
Religious groups can exploit religious freedoms to justify harmful practices.
Defending freedom of and from religion can blur the line between government neutrality toward religion and government hostility to religion.
Complete freedom from religion could marginalize cultural traditions rooted in faith.
Defending freedom of and from religion may be seen as sidelining religious expression in public life.
Defending freedom of and from religion could let secularism dominate cultural norms and make society less inclusive for religious groups.
Defending freedom of and from religion risks weakening the cultural and moral values historically rooted in religion.
Defending freedom of and from religion may foster division by putting secularism ahead of religious traditions.
Supporters need individual liberties protected and society kept harmonious.
value: Equality, personal autonomy, and democratic principles

text: Supporters need the government to stay neutral in matters of faith.
value: Equality, personal autonomy, and democratic principles

text: Opponents need dominant cultural or religious traditions upheld.
value: Societal cohesion, morality, and traditional values

text: Opponents need religious freedoms protected from what they see as secular overreach.
value: Societal cohesion, morality, and traditional values

text: The United States should stop outsourcing and become a manufacturing superpower.
Making critical goods at home reduces United States dependence on foreign nations.
Bringing manufacturing home creates high-paying jobs and strengthens the middle class.
Domestic production ensures a secure supply of essential items such as medical equipment and defense materials.
Producing more goods at home for export reduces the trade deficit.
Bringing manufacturing home encourages investment in automation and innovation so that American industry can compete globally.
The push to bring manufacturing home focuses on fair wages and better working conditions for American workers.
Curbing outsourcing reduces the exploitation of workers in low-wage countries.
A manufacturing revival promotes fair economic opportunity and reduces wealth gaps.
A manufacturing revival strengthens the United States economy in a way that benefits all citizens.
Domestic production is often more expensive because of higher wages and regulations, which raises consumer prices.
Reducing outsourcing harms economies that depend on United States contracts and could strain international relations.
The United States lacks enough skilled labor for a large-scale manufacturing revival.
Increased domestic manufacturing could lead to higher carbon emissions and resource depletion.
Protectionist policies to end outsourcing may disrupt global trade, harm international partnerships, and provoke retaliation that hurts United States exports.
Policies that discourage outsourcing may violate free trade principles.
Curbing outsourcing could harm foreign workers who depend on outsourced jobs to survive.
Domestic manufacturing could raise consumer costs in a way that falls hardest on low-income families.
Pushing to become a manufacturing superpower risks fostering nationalism at the expense of global cooperation.
Supporters need economic growth through job creation and infrastructure investment.
Supporters need national security and industrial independence protected.
Supporters need self-sufficiency, economic justice, and less reliance on foreign powers such as China.
Opponents need lower costs for goods and services, which globalization provides.
Opponents need strong international trade partnerships maintained.
Opponents need global economic interdependence and efficiency.
Ranked-choice voting produces better electoral outcomes than plurality voting.
bottom_line: The evidence gives ranked-choice voting a moderate advantage. The case that it removes the spoiler effect is strong and the record in Maine, Alaska and Australia is real; the strongest live objections are ballot exhaustion and the documented non-monotonicity failure in Burlington.

text: Ranked-choice voting eliminates the spoiler effect.
Ranked-choice voting produces winners backed by a majority of voters.
Ranked-choice voting rewards candidates who build coalitions.
Ranked-choice voting makes third parties more viable.
Ranked-choice voting causes voter confusion and ballot errors.
Under ranked-choice voting, ballots become exhausted and stop counting before the final round.
Ranked-choice voting is non-monotonic, so ranking a candidate higher can cause that candidate to lose.
Ranked-choice voting adds cost and complexity to running elections.
Maine has run statewide ranked-choice voting in federal elections since 2018 with no chaotic or fraudulent outcomes.
Australia has used preferential voting for its federal House since 1918 with stable majority outcomes.

Academic simulations find that ranked-choice voting picks the candidate who would beat every rival head to head (the Condorcet winner) about 94% of the time, compared with about 70% for plurality voting.
Roughly 15 US congressional races from 1992 to 2022 were decided by a spoiler, and ranked-choice voting would have changed several of them.
In the 2021 New York City mayoral primary, 14.9% of ballots were exhausted by the final round.
In Burlington, Vermont's 2009 election, the candidate who would have beaten every rival head to head (the Condorcet winner) was eliminated early, and voters repealed ranked-choice voting in 2010.
Australian invalid-ballot rates run 2 to 5%, which indicates a real learning curve.
Jurisdictions that adopt ranked-choice voting document higher up-front equipment, training, and tabulation costs.
Supporters of ranked-choice voting need to break the two-party lock on elections.
Supporters of ranked-choice voting need to vote sincerely without wasting their vote.
Opponents of ranked-choice voting need to protect the advantage of incumbents and major parties.
Opponents of ranked-choice voting need to keep elections cheap and simple to administer.
Voter error rates fall after the first ranked-choice voting cycle in a jurisdiction.
Jurisdictions using ranked-choice voting show more majority winners and fewer spoiler outcomes than comparable jurisdictions using plurality voting.
In a jurisdiction that adopts ranked-choice voting, the cost of running each election falls after the initial outlay for ranked-choice voting equipment.
Jurisdictions using ranked-choice voting show no rise in majority winners, persistently high ballot exhaustion, or falling turnout that does not recover.
Everyone should be treated with respect and dignity.
bottom_line: Treating people with dignity does not mean shielding them from the truth. It means inviting them into it.

text: Workers should get tax cuts, and tips should not be taxed as income.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax gives workers immediate financial relief.
Tipped workers often earn below minimum wage before tips, so cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax would help level the playing field for them.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax would leave more money in workers' pockets, which could lead to more consumer spending and economic growth.
Removing tips from taxable income makes tax filing simpler for tipped workers.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax reduces financial stress for workers whose income is already precarious.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax is consistent with the values of fairness and economic equity.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax helps close the gap between low-income and middle-income earners.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax strengthens local economies by increasing consumer spending.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax could create budget deficits for governments that rely on that revenue.
Exempting tips from tax may encourage people to underreport income or make fraudulent claims.
Exempting tips from tax could encourage tax avoidance or fraudulent reporting.
Workers in industries without tips may see exempting tips from tax as unfair preferential treatment.
Exempting tips from tax could disproportionately favor one group of workers over others.
Exempting tips from tax may create perceptions of unfairness among workers who do not receive tips.
Cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax may not significantly improve workers' overall financial stability without broader wage reforms.

Even though financial relief for workers is a good goal, cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips from tax is the wrong way to reach it, because it could undermine the tax system's equity and fiscal sustainability and create long-term economic problems.
The tax revenue lost by cutting taxes on workers and exempting tips may harm public services, and that harm would ultimately fall on the same workers.
Low-income workers need financial relief.
The economy needs the stimulation that comes from increased consumer spending.
Tipped employees need fairer treatment.
Governments need to preserve tax revenue to fund essential public services.
Workers in every income category need to be treated fairly by the tax system.
When a government pays to have software built for public services, its source code should, by default, be made public for anyone to read.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether public scrutiny of code makes it safer and cheaper, or whether it mainly helps attackers and scares off the vendors government relies on.

text: Taxpayers paid for the software that runs government services, so they should be able to see what it does, in the same way they can read the laws it enforces.
Bugs and security flaws in government software are found faster when its code is public and many outside eyes can look, and a hidden flaw in a tax or benefits system harms real people.
When one government agency publishes the code for its software, another agency can reuse it instead of paying a vendor to build the same thing again.
Publishing the code behind government software shows attackers exactly where to look, and government systems are targets that cannot afford to give their enemies a head start.
Companies that build software for government often reuse the same code for other clients, and a rule forcing it open shrinks the pool of willing suppliers.
Preparing government software code for public release costs staff time that could instead go to improving the public service the software runs.
Phone makers should be allowed to require that every app on their devices pass through an app store they review.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the protection a mandatory reviewed store offers is worth handing one company control over what everyone can install.

text: A single review checkpoint that every phone app must pass catches malware and scams before they reach millions of people who would never spot them on their own.

When every phone app must come through the phone maker's reviewed store, the maker can hold all apps to the same privacy and refund rules, so users get the same protections no matter which app they use.
When every phone app comes through one store, the phone maker is answerable for what is on it and can pull a harmful app from every phone as soon as it is discovered.
A phone maker that reviews apps and also sells its own apps competes with the developers it judges, so it can reject or delay rivals for business reasons and call it safety.
App store review by phone makers still lets harmful apps through, so the sense of safety is partly false while the loss of choice is real.
People own their phones and should decide what runs on them, just as they choose what programs to install on a personal computer, and a phone maker should not get to veto that choice after the sale.
Radio remains an essential news source during emergencies and for people who lack reliable internet access.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether radio is still the one source people can count on when power, phones, and home internet fail them, or whether phone alerts and other cheap options have taken over that job.

text: During storms, fires, and blackouts, a battery or car radio keeps working after phones die and cell towers go down.
Radio news is free to anyone with a cheap receiver, so it serves people who cannot afford a smartphone or a monthly internet bill.
Radio signals reach remote and rural areas where broadband and cell coverage are weak or missing, so for people living there it is often the only live news they can get.
Emergency alerts now push straight to most phones in an area, and that system does not depend on anyone owning a radio.
People without home internet can usually still get news from broadcast television, prepaid phones, or free access at public libraries, so radio is seldom their only option.
Consolidation of station ownership has thinned local radio newsrooms, so what comes over the air in a crisis may be national programming rather than news about the listener's own town.
Talk radio generally does more to drive its listeners apart from people who disagree with them than to inform them.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a host who speaks plainly and takes calls is giving ordinary people a voice or keeping them angry at the other side for the ratings.

text: Talk radio rewards a host who can keep listeners angry for hours, because anger holds an audience better than explanation does.
Talk radio hosts are not held to the correction and sourcing standards that newsrooms follow, so a false claim can run for weeks unchallenged.
Because a talk radio host picks which callers get on the air and can cut anyone off, listeners mostly hear the host's side win, which hardens their views instead of informing them.
Talk radio gives a platform to views that mainstream outlets ignore or dismiss, which is exactly the diversity a free press is supposed to allow.
Talk radio explains public issues in plain, everyday language, which helps listeners who find newspapers and newscasts hard to follow understand what is at stake.

Call-in shows let ordinary people speak on the air at length and disagree with the host and with each other, and hearing that open disagreement informs listeners in a way a reporter's one-sentence quote does not.
Paid random rewards in video games should be regulated the way gambling is.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether receiving a guaranteed item of uncertain value is different in kind from a bet, or different only in name.

text: Paying money for an unknown prize is the same act as pulling a slot machine lever, and calling it a game feature does not change what it does to the brain.
Paid random rewards are built into games marketed to children, who are exactly the people gambling laws exist to protect.
Game makers tune the odds and the timing of paid random reward offers to get the most spending out of players, which shows they know they are selling a chance rather than an item.
Players who buy a random reward in a game always receive something for their money, unlike a bettor who can walk away with nothing, and that difference is the legal core of what gambling means.

A random reward in a game is the same kind of purchase as a sealed pack of trading cards or a blind-bag toy, which most places sell freely to children, so putting only the game version under gambling rules would treat the same product differently just because it is digital.

Gambling regulation brings licensing, age checks and heavy compliance costs that small studios cannot bear, so treating random rewards in games as gambling would hand the market to the largest companies.
Violent content in video games generally needs no government rules beyond the age ratings the game industry already puts on its products.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether violent games do enough harm to justify rules, and whether industry age ratings already give families enough control.

text: Games have become far more violent and far more common while youth violence in most wealthy countries has not risen along with them, so there is no growing harm for new rules to fix.
Players can tell violence in a game from violence in real life, so acting out a fight on a screen does not teach them to fight in the street.
Age ratings already tell parents what a game contains, and parents who know their own children are better placed to decide what they can handle than a government office is.

Violent games reward players for violent acts over and over across thousands of hours, and repeated rewarded practice is one of the strongest ways people build habits, so the effect on players is too large to leave to an industry-run label.

Age ratings judge only the game as it ships, so they say nothing about the violent chat, videos and player-made content children run into during online play, and only outside rules can reach that gap.

Most games are now bought and downloaded online, where an age check is often just a birthdate the child types in, a gift card or a shared family account, so industry age ratings do little to keep the most violent games away from children who want them.
Popular destinations should generally cap the number of tourists they admit.
bottom_line: It turns on whether crowding is best handled by turning visitors away or by pricing them and spreading them out.

text: The more visitors a town admits, the more homes are turned into short-term rentals that price local workers out of the neighborhoods they grew up in.
Crowds wear down the very trails, old streets and monuments people come to see, so unlimited visitors destroy the thing being sold.
A town's water, roads and waste systems can serve only so many people at once, and past that point every extra visitor brings shortages and breakdowns that residents pay for.
A cap on visitor numbers makes entry scarce, and scarce entry tends to end up with whoever can pay more or book earlier, so ordinary families are the ones shut out.
Tourism is the main income for hotel workers, guides, drivers and cooks in many places, and every visitor turned away is a paycheck lost.
Spreading visitors to off-season months and quieter neighborhoods, and charging more at peak times, fixes crowding without shutting the door.
Most people probably need not cut back on their vacation flights for the climate's sake.
bottom_line: It turns on whether one person flying less matters more as a share of the world's emissions or as a signal that changes what others do.

text: Air travel is a small slice of total emissions, and one person flying less changes the total by so little that the sacrifice buys almost nothing.
The vacation flights people take now give them rest, time with faraway family and experiences they value for life, and those gains are worth more than the climate harm the flights add.
Cleaner fuels and better rules are what will actually fix aviation, and asking individuals to fly less puts the burden on travelers and lets the industry and governments off the hook.
A single long flight can outweigh many of a household's other everyday climate efforts, so how often a person flies is not a small choice within one person's life.
Cleaner planes and fuels are still far from ready at large scale, so for years to come the only way to cut the pollution from vacation flights is for people to take fewer of them.
When many people choose to fly less for the climate, airlines and governments respond to what travelers demand, so cutting back on vacation flights is how the larger climate fixes get started.
We should tax property by the value of the land itself, independent of what is or is not built on it.
bottom_line: The evidence indicates significant promise if a land value tax is done right, and significant pitfalls if it is done poorly.

text: Taxing land whether or not it is developed encourages efficient land use and discourages holding land for speculation.
A land value tax discourages leaving land idle by creating immediate carrying costs for vacant or underused properties.
A land value tax removes the incentive to hold prime locations without developing them.
A land value tax pushes landowners to make the most productive use of their land or sell it to someone who will.
A land value tax is a fair revenue source because it captures value created by public investment instead of taxing labor or capital.
A land value tax returns land value increases generated by the community to the public that created them.
A land value tax reduces free-riding by landowners who benefit from public infrastructure without contributing to it.
A land value tax creates a more economically efficient tax base that causes very little economic waste (deadweight loss).
A land value tax can lower housing costs by encouraging development of underused land, which increases housing supply.
A land value tax mobilizes vacant and underused parcels for development.
A land value tax reduces the artificial land scarcity that drives up prices.
A land value tax eliminates tax penalties on building improvements that add to the housing stock.
A land value tax avoids the distortions found in most other forms of taxation.
A land value tax does not penalize or discourage productive economic activity.
A land value tax cannot be avoided through offshoring or accounting practices.
A land value tax aligns private economic incentives with the land use that is best for society.
Under a land value tax, building new homes or businesses does not raise the owner's tax bill, which can spur construction and renovation.
Holding idle land costs money under a land value tax, which deters investors from sitting on vacant land waiting for its value to rise.
Much of a land's value comes from the community rather than the owner's efforts, so taxing land value recovers unearned value for public use.
Land cannot be hidden or moved and taxing it does not reduce the supply of land, so a land tax is hard to evade and causes less economic distortion.
A land value tax provides a steady revenue base for local governments to fund services.
Accurately assessing unimproved land value separately from buildings is contentious and technically difficult, which makes a land value tax hard to administer.
A land value tax requires sophisticated and ongoing valuation systems.
A land value tax creates potential for assessment disputes and litigation.
A land value tax may involve prohibitive administrative costs in areas without existing assessment capacity.
A land value tax may create significant financial hardship for low-income landowners in areas with high land values who have limited cash flow to pay it.
A land value tax forces farmers near developing areas to intensify production or sell their farmland.
A land value tax creates impossible tax burdens for elderly homeowners on fixed incomes in appreciating neighborhoods.
A land value tax disconnects tax obligations from ability to pay, particularly for residential owners.
A land value tax risks unintended consequences such as rapid gentrification, community displacement, or environmentally harmful overdevelopment.
A land value tax accelerates neighborhood turnover and could destroy established communities.
A land value tax creates pressure to develop natural areas or open spaces that have development potential.
A land value tax may encourage rushed, poor-quality development to generate immediate income.
A land value tax faces substantial political obstacles from entrenched interests and from concerns about dramatic shifts in who pays.
Resistance from powerful landowners makes a land value tax hard to enact.
A land value tax faces political resistance because it challenges deeply held beliefs about property rights.
A land value tax is politically hard to pass because its losses fall heavily on specific groups while its benefits are spread thinly across many people.
Mistakes or infrequent updates in land valuation can lead to unfair taxes or sudden changes in tax bills.
Rapid increases in land value could produce steep tax hikes that force owners who cannot afford the new tax to sell or move.
Some regions have laws requiring uniform property taxes, which complicates a land-only tax.
A land value tax set very high could discourage development or investment in some cases.
A land value tax will likely lower market land values, so current landowners lose some of their wealth.
If only one city or region adopts a land value tax, landowners may lobby against local improvements that would raise their land values.
A land value tax has not been widely adopted in modern times, which suggests that real-world constraints and pushback have kept it rare.
In Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, which taxed land at a higher rate than buildings, the number of vacant structures dropped from over 4,200 in 1982 to under 500 by 2001.
Harrisburg's mayor credited the land-focused tax as one key factor in attracting over $1.2 billion in new investment and reversing decades of decline.
After Allentown, Pennsylvania shifted to a land-heavy tax, 70% of homeowners got a tax cut and building permits in previously stagnant neighborhoods increased by 32%.
After Allentown voters approved taxing land at five times the rate on buildings in the mid-1990s, the city did not need to raise taxes for several years.
When several Pennsylvania cities adopted a land-weighted tax, absentee owners of vacant lots shouldered much more of the burden while many homeowners and active businesses saw tax cuts.
Milton Friedman called a tax on unimproved land the least bad tax.
The IMF and the OECD have supported land value taxation in principle as a tax that does not hinder economic activity.
The Mirrlees Review of the UK tax system recommended land value taxation as a sensible reform.
An economic model suggested that replacing other taxes with a combination of a land tax and a consumption tax could significantly boost economic output.
Studies of Pittsburgh's split-rate tax, in place from 1913 to 2001, found that it encouraged building activity in the city.

Estonia's national land tax, introduced in the 1990s and still funding local governments today, is cited as a relatively successful implementation, though at modest rates and not without controversies over valuation.
A 2001 reassessment in Pittsburgh sharply raised assessed land values, homeowners got unexpected tax hikes, and the city repealed its two-rate tax that year.
In built-up neighborhoods land rarely sells on its own, so assessors must estimate how much of each property's value comes from the land versus the structure.
In the UK, a proposal to consider land value taxation was attacked as a tax on gardens, which made politicians wary.
Numerous UK studies and commissions have recommended a land value tax, yet the political will to adopt one has been lacking.
Supporters need sustainable urban development.
Supporters need housing to be more affordable and easier to access.
Supporters need wealth inequality reduced through more equitable taxation.
Supporters need tax systems that are economically efficient.
Opponents need traditional ownership models protected.
Opponents need asset-rich, cash-poor owners protected from financial hardship.
Opponents need agricultural and rural land to stay viable.
Opponents need community stability preserved and displacement prevented.
Competition in educational opportunities, such as charter schools and school vouchers, makes traditional public schools better.

Monopolies can stifle innovation and efficiency in any industry, and allowing competition in education encourages traditional public schools to improve and adapt to meet students' needs more effectively.
When parents and kids are free to choose their school, everyone benefits.

Just as competition from UPS and FedEx led to improvements in the USPS, Airbus makes Boeing better, and Toyota made Ford build more fuel-efficient cars, competition in education encourages all educational institutions to raise their standards.
Competition drives schools to excel and innovate, benefiting the people they serve, just as it does for sports teams and for the automotive and aerospace industries.
Introducing competition into education can foster an adversarial us-versus-them mentality that puts winning ahead of cooperative learning and community building.
A competitive framework in education might not only divide communities but also lead to heightened tensions and conflicts that detract from the educational experience and its goals.
Empirical studies show that school vouchers lead to improvements in public schools because of the competitive pressure they create.
In areas where charter schools and vouchers are common, public schools often see a decrease in funding, which hurts their ability to provide quality education and maintain infrastructure.
Supporters need excellence to be valued over equality.
Supporters need at least the motivated students to be able to escape broken schools.
Supporters need schools to compete for students as a driver of excellence.
Supporters need competition to push schools to improve teaching methods, curricula, and student services in order to attract and keep students.
Supporters need parents and students to have the freedom to choose schools that best meet their educational needs and preferences rather than being confined to schools based on where they live.
Supporters need innovative teaching practices and technologies to be introduced and spread, which they believe happens more readily in competitive environments.
Supporters need schools to be accountable for student outcomes and to be efficient and responsive to community needs.
Supporters need free-market principles to be trusted to drive innovation and improvement.
Supporters need relief from what they see as the inefficiencies and rigidities of traditional public school systems.
Supporters need a school system that adequately prepares students for future success, which they believe the current system fails to do.
Opponents need equality to be valued over potential excellence.
Opponents need to avoid all the motivated students going to charter schools and leaving less motivated students behind.
Opponents need education to remain a field without competition, which is part of why they entered it.

Opponents need public schools to keep the funding that charter schools and voucher programs would draw away, because that loss falls hardest on schools in low-income areas and widens the gap in educational quality between affluent and disadvantaged communities.
Opponents need public schools to remain community hubs where students from diverse backgrounds learn together rather than being sorted by class, race, or religion.
Opponents need taxpayer money to stay with schools that have transparent accountability rather than shift to private entities with less oversight.

Opponents need essential services that public schools are required to provide, such as special education, free or reduced-price meals, and psychological counseling, to stay uniformly available to all students, especially those with special needs, which they fear a competitive school system might not ensure.
Opponents need education not to be privatized or turned into a commodity.
Opponents need resources and attention to stay focused on improving all public schools.
Opponents need education to be treated as a public good controlled by democratically accountable institutions.
Opponents need educational opportunities not to become more segregated and unequal.
America should adopt a comprehensive scorecard that measures national progress across human development, economic vitality, environmental health, and social cohesion, not just GDP.
bottom_line: The American Scorecard addresses a real problem, the limits of GDP, with a comprehensive solution, but its success depends on careful implementation, institutional safeguards, and sustained political will.

text: GDP measures economic activity, not human well-being, and its own architect warned against using it as a measure of welfare.
Comprehensive metrics reveal declining national vital signs that GDP growth hides.
A comprehensive scorecard would enable evidence-based policymaking, and decisions driven by data are better than decisions driven by ideology.
Clear metrics let citizens judge how well their leaders are performing.
Surveys show that people care more about health, happiness, and community than about GDP.
Other nations that use broader measures of progress have seen their policies improve.
A comprehensive scorecard is too complex for the public and policymakers to use effectively.
Many of the proposed metrics are hard to measure objectively or consistently.
A comprehensive scorecard would become a political football rather than an objective tool.
Creating and maintaining a comprehensive measurement system would be expensive and bureaucratic.
A scorecard would only measure problems without addressing their root causes, because knowing problems exist does not solve them without actual policy changes.
GDP has flaws, but it already provides a consistent, internationally comparable measure.
Simon Kuznets, GDP's architect, is quoted as saying that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income.
In the United States, GDP has risen while life expectancy has fallen.
Stock market gains are concentrated while median household wealth is stagnant.
Spending on environmental cleanup counts as GDP growth, so environmental damage can show up as growth.
U.S. life expectancy declined from 2015 to 2017 and declined sharply from 2020 to 2022.
Infant mortality rates in the United States are higher than those of peer nations.
Social trust in the United States is at historic lows.
U.S. infrastructure is crumbling even though the U.S. economy has grown.
Countries that use broader measures of progress, such as Bhutan's Gross National Happiness and New Zealand's Living Standards Framework, report better policy alignment.
Studies in business and education find that performance metrics increase accountability.
Happiness research finds that relationships, health, and purpose matter more than income once income passes a certain level.
Research on information overload finds that adding more information yields diminishing returns.
Survey-based metrics are subject to response bias.
GDP methodology is standardized across the world.
GDP makes historical comparisons possible.
Citizens need better visibility into real well-being, policies that match their needs, and stronger democratic accountability.
Vulnerable populations need mental health, substance abuse, and poverty made visible, and need policy attention to overlooked problems.
Future generations need environmental sustainability and debt sustainability tracked and long-term thinking encouraged.
Local communities need their infrastructure and livability measured, their community engagement valued, and their regional differences made visible.
Reform-minded politicians need evidence for their policy priorities, an accountability tool, and a counter to a pure GDP focus.
Politicians invested in the status quo need to avoid added accountability and keep performance failures from becoming visible.
Businesses focused on short-term GDP need to keep their environmental and social costs from being made visible and to avoid pressure for sustainable practices.
Ideological extremes need to protect purely ideological positions that an evidence-based approach would threaten.
Government agencies facing scrutiny need to avoid having performance failures exposed and new resource demands placed on them.
A good end does not justify using means that would otherwise be wrong.
bottom_line: The claim is strongest understood as a default rule that blocks self-serving excuses, not as an absolute ban that overrides all judgment about context. The alternative, judging actions by their outcomes alone, performs far worse in both theory and practice.

text: In a society with laws, a person's goals do not justify breaking the law to reach them.
Both the goals and the methods of an action must be judged, not only the outcome.
Having specific rules about acceptable methods produces better outcomes than telling everyone to judge by results.
A person who relies on the law for protection but breaks it for their own vision of the greater good is a hypocrite.
If everyone believed the ends justify the means, the world would be dramatically worse.
Calculating the final result of all of one's actions is impossible, so rules about methods produce good outcomes more reliably than judging each case by its expected results.

If the ends justify the means, there is no meaningful difference between consequences that are foreseen and consequences that are intended, which would erase the distinctions between negligence, recklessness, and intent that any working justice system depends on.

Selfish goals do not justify actions that hurt others, and most people who say the ends justify the means are not pursuing humanity's greatest good but rationalizing something they already wanted to do.
That some extreme cases, such as lethal force in genuine self-defense, change which methods are justified does not show that all ends justify all means.
God will not require people to do evil in order to defeat evil.
Sometimes the ends do justify the means, because a blanket rule against it ignores morally relevant facts about the size of the harm, the chance of success, and the alternatives available.
The worst mass killings of the 20th century (Soviet collectivization, the Maoist purges, the Holocaust) were carried out by people who genuinely believed they were pursuing a necessary good.
John Stuart Mill's rule utilitarianism holds that following rules produces better long-run outcomes than judging each act by its consequences, because rules resist self-serving rationalization.

Under social contract theory (Locke, Hobbes, Rawls), constitutional government rests on the idea that people give up some freedom to act by any means they choose in exchange for legal protection, so reasoning that the ends justify the means is a one-sided breach of that contract.
Research on motivated reasoning consistently shows that people are much better at spotting ends-justify-the-means reasoning in their opponents than in themselves.
Philosophers from Foot to Thomson have built trolley problem and lifeboat scenarios in which strict adherence to rules about methods produces outcomes that almost everyone judges as worse.

Just War Theory, endorsed by international law, most religious traditions, and nearly all moral philosophers, holds that some ends such as stopping genocide or repelling invasion can justify killing that would otherwise be prohibited.
Rosa Parks and Gandhi broke the law, and most people now judge their illegal methods as justified by their goals.
Supporters need to live under a predictable rule of law that protects everyone equally.
Supporters need protection from being treated as an acceptable casualty of someone else's greater good.
Supporters need moral systems that cannot be easily gamed by anyone who claims good intentions.
Supporters need principled constraints on methods, rather than case-by-case calculation, for the sake of better long-run outcomes.
Opponents need the flexibility to respond to genuine moral emergencies.
Opponents need rules that do not produce obviously bad outcomes in edge cases.
Opponents need a moral philosophy that matches moral intuition in extreme situations.
Opponents need to keep rigid rule-following from becoming a form of moral cowardice ("I was just following the rules").
Movements and regimes that adopt explicit ends-justify-the-means doctrines show higher rates of atrocity and abuse than comparable rule-constrained ones.
Coercive methods justified as emergency necessity, such as torture for time-sensitive intelligence, produce unreliable intelligence on the whole.
Institutions granted emergency exception powers expand their use beyond the original emergency.
People rate identical ends-justify-the-means actions as more acceptable when their own side performs them.
Rule-bound institutions outperform discretionary ones on long-run outcomes and on resistance to capture.
Some identifiable class of agents reliably predicts consequences accurately enough that judging by outcomes alone beats following rules.
Removing a constraint on methods in a real domain demonstrably improves outcomes without increasing abuse.
Emergency exception powers, once granted, do not expand beyond their original justification.
We should defend the United States Constitution.
The Constitution's counter-majoritarian features entrench minority preferences regardless of whether those preferences are good ideas.
The ratification of the 13th, 17th, 19th, and 21st Amendments shows the system has repeatedly repaired fundamental errors through its own amendment channel.

The United States has had roughly 250 years of mostly peaceful transfers of power, which is rare among written constitutions, and this shows that when losing is survivable, fights over who takes power next turn into campaigns.

State policy experiments spread to other states when their results are positive, which shows that the states really do work as laboratories for testing policies under the Constitution's split of power.
No amendment proposed after 1971 has been ratified, and the 27th Amendment took 203 years, so the repair channel may be frozen under modern polarization.
Most presidential constitutions modeled on the US design collapsed into instability or autocracy, so the design travels badly.
Democratic backsliding proceeds inside formally intact constitutional structures, so a written constitution without supporting norms does not hold.
Supporters need the rule of law and stability.
Supporters need liberty secured through distributed power.
Opponents need justice and equality.
Opponents need government that responds to actual majorities.
Congressional term limits would reduce corruption and improve legislative quality.
bottom_line: The evidence moderately supports the view that term limits reduce entrenched corruption, but the gains from incumbents' weaker fundraising position and a shorter time to build relationships may be offset by more inexperienced legislators and more lobbyist influence.

text: Term limits weaken incumbents' fundraising advantage, which reduces their dependence on corporate and special-interest donors.
Term limits end the practice of donors investing in decade-long relationships with powerful committee chairs in expectation of returns.
Term limits do not eliminate PAC influence, because non-incumbent candidates attract outside spending just as much and the money only shifts toward open-seat races.
Inexperienced legislators are more vulnerable to lobbying and staff manipulation, so term limits increase dependence on outside expertise and lobbyist guidance.
Legislators serving a final term imposed by term limits face fewer accountability constraints and may accept bribes without consequence, so term limits increase the risk of corruption.
Presidential term limits under the 22nd Amendment succeeded in preventing the concentration of executive power, showing that fixed term limits can reduce the incentive to cling to power corruptly.

A cross-state analysis of U.S. governors' term limits found that stricter limits were associated with a lower overall magnitude of corruption, and that shorter tenures impede the formation of extensive corrupt networks.

Term-limited state legislatures in Michigan, Ohio and Arkansas saw seniority shift to staff rather than legislators, with reduced deliberative capacity and greater dependence on lobbyist briefings for policy expertise.

After the 1994 Republican "revolution," a class of new U.S. House members with ideological purity but weaker institutional experience led to gridlock and ineffective legislation, which cuts against the idea that term limits improve legislative quality.

Under Mexico's no-reelection rule, legislators could not serve consecutive terms, which made them lame ducks with an even higher risk of corruption and weakened their incentive to build a legislative reputation.
A theoretical model shows that legislators with known expiration dates have weaker reputational constraints, predicting that moral hazard and corruption increase as a term limit approaches.

Term limits increase polarization in state legislatures, with larger effects in more professional legislatures, and in term-limited states party committees increased their contributions to candidates, which intensified partisanship.
Supporters need money's influence in politics reduced by weakening incumbents' fundraising power.
Supporters need opportunities for challenger candidates, especially younger and minority candidates shut out by seniority systems.
Supporters need to prevent one party from becoming entrenched in safe districts.
Supporters need to restore a citizen legislature of part-time, non-professional politicians.
Some Republican supporters need the partisan advantage that comes from Democratic retirements in marginal districts.
Opponents need to protect voters' right to reelect effective representatives for as long as they choose.
Opponents need legislative expertise and institutional knowledge preserved for competent lawmaking.
Opponents need to prevent the lame-duck problem in which legislators with nothing to lose act without consequence.
Opponents need continuity in committee leadership and in advocacy for district interests.
Sitting legislators need to keep their seats, so they oppose any rule that threatens them.
Term-limited state legislatures show measurably lower corruption conviction rates than states without term limits, after controlling for size and party composition.
First-term legislators commit quid pro quo corruption at lower rates than legislators who have served several terms.
After term limits take effect, lobbyist access to legislators decreases rather than increases.
Within five years after term limits are put in place, federal corruption convictions decline by 30 to 50 percent.
In the first election cycle after term limits are put in place, incumbents' fundraising advantage over challengers narrows by 40 to 60 percent.
Term-limited legislatures show equal or higher corruption rates than legislatures without term limits.
Lame-duck legislators commit corruption at higher rates than first-term members.
Lobbyist influence or PAC contributions increase disproportionately after term limits take effect.
After term limits take effect, legislative output and quality decline significantly, and other reforms do not make up for the loss.
Mexico's experience under its strict no-reelection rule shows no reduction in corruption.
Representative civic juries should be convened, online and in person, to deliberate on key legislation.
bottom_line: Give people facts, time, and structured debate, and democracy actually works.

text: Civic juries replace shallow opinion polls with deep deliberation.
Civic juries give citizens a way to provide structured input continuously, not only at elections.
Civic juries let citizens participate meaningfully whenever they choose to contribute.
Civic juries give randomly selected, demographically representative jurors time, expert briefings, and structured deliberation so they can move from gut reactions to informed judgment.
Civic juries make it harder for elected officials to ignore documented public reasoning.
Online civic juries let thousands of people contribute.
Online civic juries produce better collective intelligence by bringing in more perspectives.
Broader representation gives a civic jury's recommendations greater legitimacy.
Civic juries aim for transparent reasoning rather than consensus, so elected officials and voters can see why people support or oppose policies.
Mongolia used deliberative polling to gather public input on constitutional reforms, and Parliament wrote the process into national law as a permanent part of its constitutional amendment process.
Ireland's Citizens' Assembly of 99 randomly selected citizens deliberated on abortion rights, and a constitutional referendum driven by its recommendations legalized abortion.
Ireland legalized same-sex marriage through a constitutional referendum driven by citizen assembly recommendations.
In the 2019 America in One Room experiment, political polarization dropped measurably among more than 500 demographically diverse Americans after a weekend of structured deliberation.
In the 2019 America in One Room experiment, participants' empathy for opposing viewpoints increased after a weekend of structured deliberation.
In the 2019 America in One Room experiment, participants shifted positions based on evidence rather than tribal loyalty.
In the 2019 America in One Room experiment, both conservative and liberal participants moderated extreme positions.
Ireland's 2024 referendums on family definitions failed despite citizen assembly recommendations.
True freedom requires balancing individual liberty with personal responsibility and active civic engagement.
bottom_line: None of the three principles (liberty, responsibility, engagement) works without the others.

text: Liberty, personal responsibility and civic engagement each become distorted when pursued on their own.
Liberty without responsibility turns into lawlessness, meaning freedom that contributes nothing and has no connection to other people.
When responsibility is cut loose from liberty, the slogan "personal responsibility" gets used as a weapon to justify privilege and concentrate authority.
Absolute liberty without shared rules produces chaos in which only the powerful thrive.
Public policy should be driven by data and measurable outcomes rather than by ideology.
bottom_line: There is a strong case for evidence as a necessary input to policy, and there are significant, legitimate objections to naive data-driven frameworks that ignore values, local knowledge, and data capture. The disagreement is rarely about whether data should matter; it is about which data, who interprets it, and whether "evidence-based" is a neutral standard or a rhetorical weapon.

text: Policies with measurable outcomes can be corrected when they fail, and policies without them cannot.
The track record of ideology-driven policy, across the political spectrum, is substantially worse than that of evidence-driven alternatives.
Good policy ideas come from all parts of the political spectrum, and filtering ideas by ideology discards them.
When the reasoning behind a policy is laid out openly, with each claim linked to its evidence and the quality of that evidence shown, motivated reasoning becomes visible and can be corrected.
Voters can only hold officials accountable for outcomes they can measure.
The label "evidence-based" is regularly used as a rhetorical weapon to favor some kinds of knowledge over others.
Most major policy disagreements are about values rather than facts, and data cannot resolve disputes about values.
Data-driven policy systems can be captured by the people who generate and control the data.
Measurable outcomes create their own distortions, because when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure (Goodhart's Law).

Expert consensus has been wrong on important questions, sometimes systematically, so policy frameworks that defer excessively to it build in a systematic lag before correcting errors that independent political pressure might have caught sooner.

The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, a standing body that reviews evidence and issues binding recommendations based on cost-effectiveness, is documented to save the NHS about 1.5 billion pounds a year compared with unevaluated adoption of new treatments, while improving patient outcomes.
Education programs rated "strong evidence" by the U.S. Department of Education's What Works Clearinghouse consistently outperform programs without evidence ratings.

Police departments that use data-driven deployment (crime hotspot analysis and predictive resource allocation) achieve measurably better crime reduction per dollar than departments using traditional patrol methods, with effect sizes of 15 to 30 percent in controlled comparisons.

Cochrane Reviews and meta-analyses of pharmaceutical research consistently find that industry-funded studies produce favorable results at two to three times the rate of independent studies of the same treatments.

Measuring that a policy has failed does not by itself get the policy corrected: crime prevention programs such as D.A.R.E., Scared Straight and boot camps for juvenile offenders showed no effect or harmful effects in rigorous evaluations, yet kept running for decades on political popularity.
Citizens frustrated by gridlock and ideological performance need government to solve the problems it says it will solve.
Fiscally minded voters need demonstrated value for government spending.
Reform-oriented politicians need an evidence standard to justify cross-partisan positions.
Policy researchers and evaluation professionals need frameworks that validate their expertise, which evidence-based policy does.
value: Humility about what we know, Professional standing

value: Humility about what we know, Self-interest
